entities.name: Late Medieval
entities.label: Timeframe
entities.summary:
The Late Medieval period, roughly spanning from 1300 to 1500 CE, represents a profound era of crisis, transformation, and eventual renewal across Eurasia and parts of Africa, fundamentally reshaping the trajectory of world history. This timeframe, distinct from the High Middle Ages, witnessed the unraveling of established feudal and ecclesiastical structures, giving way to the nascent forms of the modern world. It was a period defined by immense demographic catastrophe, protracted warfare, religious schism, and significant intellectual and technological innovation, laying the groundwork for the Renaissance and the Age of Exploration.

Key events of the Late Medieval era include the devastating Black Death (1346–1353), which annihilated an estimated 30-60% of Europe's population and caused widespread social and economic upheaval, impacting labor markets and class structures from England to Egypt. Concurrently, Europe was wracked by the Hundred Years' War (1337–1453) between England and France, which fostered early national identities and transformed military tactics. The Western Schism (1378–1417) saw multiple competing popes, severely undermining papal authority, while the Ottoman Empire's expansion culminated in the Fall of Constantinople in 1453, ending the Byzantine Empire and shifting geopolitical power. Across the globe, the Ming Dynasty in China saw significant cultural and economic flourishing, including Zheng He's maritime expeditions (1405–1433), demonstrating sophisticated naval power and diplomatic reach.
